claims.text: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low hardness and strength.
The relatively low hardness and strength of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi are governed by its homogeneous simple solid-solution structure.
The simple solid-solution structure lacks nanoscale precipitates.
The simple solid-solution structure lacks short-range ordering.
The absence of nanoscale precipitates or short-range ordering produces low lattice friction and minimal obstruction of dislocations.
Low lattice friction and minimal dislocation obstruction favor plastic deformation and machinability.
Fine precipitates or short-range-ordered domains can hinder dislocation glide.
Nanoscale particles that obstruct dislocation motion increase hardness.
Nanoscale particles that obstruct dislocation motion increase compressive strength.
Easy dislocation glide in simple-solid-solution CoCrFeNiTi promotes good plasticity.
Easy dislocation glide in simple-solid-solution CoCrFeNiTi promotes machinability.
Introducing nanoscale precipitates should increase hardness relative to the homogenized baseline.
Introducing nanoscale precipitates should increase yield strength relative to the homogenized baseline.
Precipitation strengthening may reduce ductility relative to the baseline.
Unmodified homogenized CoCrFeNiTi should retain lower hardness and strength but superior plasticity relative to the precipitate-containing condition.
The proposed mechanism applies to near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi from approximately 25 °C to 600 °C under tensile and compressive loading near yield.
Moving farther from near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi could introduce additional strengthening mechanisms.
A tailored heat treatment can be used to induce nanoscale precipitation in CoCrFeNiTi.
